paras: The attempted lynching of Charles Smith took place in East Liverpool, Ohio, early on May 21, 1888, when about five hundred people surrounded the City Hall where Smith, a Black man accused of assaulting a 12-year-old girl, was held. Officers barred the doors, the crowd dispersed, and Smith was committed to jail the same day.

According to an East Liverpool dispatch, Angelica O'Hanlon, 12, was walking with her ten-year-old brother on the Lisbon road on the evening of May 20 when "a colored man named Charles Smith" attacked her. The dispatch said he tried to rape her, fought off her brother, and fled.

Officers and citizens set out after Smith, and a policeman caught him in a wood after, by this account, Smith drew a razor. On the way to the jail the officer "several times had to face the mob and beat them back." At one o'clock the next morning about five hundred people surrounded the City Hall, where all the officers were inside behind barred doors. The Wheeling Register reported that the mob "lacked a leader," so its cries of "Lynch him" came to nothing.

Some two hundred people crowded into Smith's preliminary hearing at noon, where the girl's brother, Dave O'Hanlon, tried to attack him and was held back. The Mayor hurried the hearing and committed Smith to jail in default of $5,000 bail. No report of a trial or later outcome appears in the coverage, and no one in the crowd is reported arrested.

Two white papers carried the same dispatch on May 21. The Springfield Daily Republic ran the shorter version as "A Negro Rapes a Girl," ending with Smith's arrest and the remark that "it is thought he will be mobbed." The Wheeling Register printed the fuller version under "A COLORED RAPIST" and the deck "In Danger of His Life at East Liverpool—A Revolting Crime." Both papers told the accusation as fact and called Smith "the brute"; neither criticized the crowd, and the Wheeling text credited the officer with saving "his man."

bases: A crowd of about five hundred surrounded the East Liverpool City Hall where the accused Charles Smith was held, crying "Lynch him," after an officer had to beat back a mob on the way to the jail; no one was killed (A1, A2).

A mob of about five hundred sought Smith, accused of assaulting a girl, with cries of "Lynch him," but the doors were barred and he was held and committed for trial, so no killing occurred; this was an attempted lynching (A1).

The two reports print the same East Liverpool dispatch on the assault accusation, and only the Wheeling Register (A1) carries the mob at the jail and City Hall; the Springfield text (A2) says only that Smith was arrested and was expected to be mobbed.

accounts.label: East Liverpool dispatch (fuller version)
accounts.gist: Smith, accused of assaulting a 12-year-old girl, was caught in a wood after drawing a razor; a mob was beaten back on the way to jail, five hundred surrounded City Hall at 1 a.m. but lacked a leader, and Smith was committed in default of $5,000 bail.

accounts.label: East Liverpool dispatch (shorter version)
accounts.gist: The same assault account, ending with Smith's arrest and the expectation that 'he will be mobbed.'

framing.detail: The Wheeling Register headlined 'A COLORED RAPIST / In Danger of His Life at East Liverpool—A Revolting Crime,' told the accusation as fact, and called Smith 'the brute' and 'the negro.'
The Springfield Daily Republic headlined 'A Negro Rapes a Girl' and repeated the accusation as fact, noting that 'it is thought he will be mobbed.'

conflicts.note: A1 appeared in the May 21 issue and speaks of 'this morning,' so its 'May 29' dateline is a misprint or OCR error; May 21 fits both issue dates.

info: Assault alleged 'late last evening' (evening of May 20, 1888); the crowd surrounded City Hall at 1 a.m. the following morning (May 21) and the hearing was held at noon that day
